body:
---

## Summary

The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) operates a state-sponsored employment fraud program in which North Korean IT workers — often operating from China, Russia, and Southeast Asia — use stolen or synthetic American identities to fraudulently obtain remote employment at Western technology companies. The program generates revenue for the North Korean regime in violation of international sanctions, while simultaneously creating insider threat vectors for credential theft, source code exfiltration, and post-termination data extortion. The DOJ has documented 136+ compromised U.S. companies with $2.2M+ in direct salary revenue from a single case, while CrowdStrike has observed 304 incidents. The threat has escalated since mid-2024 from pure salary extraction to active data exfiltration and ransom demands, representing a convergence of state-sponsored espionage, employment fraud, and cyber extortion. The operation relies on organized facilitator networks spanning the U.S. and Ukraine that provide stolen identities, proxy laptop hosting at U.S. addresses, and financial laundering infrastructure.

The World Cybercrime Index (Bruce et al., PLoS ONE 2024) provides independent academic corroboration: North Korea ranks #7 globally (WCI 10.61/100) with a pronounced attacks/extortion specialization (25.33 — 2.4x its overall score), while scoring minimally on scams (2.17) and cash-out (3.88). This asymmetric profile reflects a state-directed cybercrime apparatus focused on high-impact attacks rather than the broad-spectrum fraud production seen in other top-ranked countries. Note: WCI data was collected in 2021, before the IT worker fraud campaign reached its current documented scale.

---

| WCI Attacks/Extortion — North Korea | 25.33/100 (pronounced specialization) | World Cybercrime Index (Bruce et al. 2024) | 2021 data |
| WCI Scams — North Korea | 2.17/100 (minimal) | World Cybercrime Index (Bruce et al. 2024) | 2021 data |
| WCI Technical Products — North Korea | 8.66/100 | World Cybercrime Index (Bruce et al. 2024) | 2021 data |

---

## Threat Path Hypothesis

> **Hypothesis**: DPRK state-sponsored IT workers are using organized facilitator networks to obtain stolen U.S. identities, fraudulently secure remote software engineering positions at Western companies, extract salary revenue for the North Korean regime, and increasingly exfiltrate proprietary source code and credentials for use in extortion and intelligence operations.

**Confidence**: Very High — confirmed by multiple independent law enforcement actions (FBI IC3 PSAs January 2025 and July 2025, DOJ enforcement actions January and November 2025), threat intelligence vendors (Google, Microsoft "Jasper Sleet," CrowdStrike, Palo Alto Unit 42, SentinelOne), and international government advisories.

**Estimated Impact**: $50,000 – $300,000+ per placement per year (salary extraction); $500K – $5M+ per extortion event (proprietary code/data ransom); aggregate regime revenue estimated at $500M/year across 100,000+ operatives in 40+ countries (Flare/IBM X-Force, March 2026), with individual operators earning $300,000+ annually. Secondary impacts include sanctions compliance liability for employing entities, intellectual property loss, and credential compromise enabling follow-on cyber operations.

---

## CFPF Phase Mapping

### Phase 1: Recon

| Technique | Description | Indicators |
|-----------|-------------|------------|
| CFPF-P1-001: Facilitator network activation | DPRK operators activate U.S.- and Ukraine-based facilitator networks to procure stolen American identities, including SSNs, driver's licenses, and residential addresses. Known facilitators include identity theft ring operators and U.S. nationals who sell or rent their identities. | Facilitator patterns: multiple unrelated individuals using the same residential address for employment; identity documents with metadata inconsistencies |
| CFPF-P1-002: Synthetic credential fabrication | Operators create fabricated resumes, LinkedIn profiles, and GitHub portfolios using stolen identities. AI tools (including ChatGPT) are used to generate interview preparation materials and enhance credential documents. Education credentials typically list non-North American universities (Singapore, Japan, Hong Kong) paired with U.S. addresses. | LinkedIn profiles with limited connection history and recent creation dates; GitHub repositories with unusual commit patterns; resumes combining U.S. addresses with non-North American education |
| CFPF-P1-003: Proxy infrastructure setup | U.S.-based accomplices host laptops at American residential addresses to create the appearance of domestic work. Operators connect remotely via Astrill VPN and remote desktop tools (AnyDesk, TeamViewer) to these proxy machines. | Laptop farm indicators: multiple active sessions on single residential IP; remote management tool installations on employer-provisioned hardware; Astrill VPN connections |
| CFPF-P1-004: Target employer reconnaissance | Operators identify companies with remote-first hiring, minimal in-person vetting, and software engineering openings. Technology companies, fintech firms, and crypto exchanges are primary targets. Staffing platforms (Upwork, Fiverr, Toptal) are also used. | N/A (external reconnaissance not directly observable by target companies) |
| CFPF-P1-005: Internal DPRK management platform coordination | Operators coordinate via internal DPRK platforms named "RB Site" and "NetkeyRegister" which serve as management dashboards for tracking placements, assignments, and revenue across the program. OConnect VPN and NetKey VPN are used for connections back to Pyongyang network infrastructure. IP Messenger is used for internal communications between operators and controllers. (Source: Flare/IBM X-Force, March 2026) | OConnect VPN connection signatures; NetKey VPN traffic patterns; IP Messenger protocol traffic; connections to DPRK network infrastructure from endpoints also connected to corporate VPN |
| CFPF-P1-006: Western collaborator recruitment | Western collaborators are recruited via LinkedIn and GitHub for identity lending — knowingly providing their legitimate identities for employment applications in exchange for ongoing compensation (percentage of salary). This is distinct from stolen identity procurement: collaborator-enabled placements use genuine identity documents, making them significantly harder to detect through standard identity verification. (Source: Flare/IBM X-Force, March 2026) | LinkedIn/GitHub recruitment messages offering compensation for identity lending; same individual's identity documents associated with multiple concurrent employment relationships; salary payments split between employee account and separate "collaborator" account |

**Data Sources**: Identity verification services, resume screening systems, LinkedIn profile analytics, VPN/proxy detection services, device management logs, background check vendor data.

---

### Phase 2: Initial Access

| Technique | Description | Indicators |
|-----------|-------------|------------|
| CFPF-P2-001: Fraudulent job application | Operators submit job applications using stolen identities through company career portals, staffing agencies, and freelance platforms. Resumes are tailored to match job requirements using AI-generated content. Multiple operators may apply to the same company using different stolen identities. | Applications from candidates whose background checks reveal address/identity inconsistencies; multiple applicants sharing device fingerprints or IP infrastructure; resume content that closely mirrors job description language |
| CFPF-P2-002: Interview performance via AI assistance and face/voice changers | Operators perform well in technical interviews using ChatGPT and AI coding assistants for real-time answer generation. Video interviews may use dedicated AI face changers and AI voice changers providing real-time transformation during live video calls — not just static deepfake overlays but continuous face/voice transformation tools (Flare/IBM X-Force, March 2026). Multiple operators may tag-team interview stages. Candidates also take malicious coding challenges on corporate devices, compromising their employers — particularly IT staff augmentation services (Recorded Future CTA-2026-0319). | Candidates who refuse or repeatedly reschedule video interviews; notable discrepancy between interview performance and subsequent job performance; audio/video artifacts suggesting AI generation or real-time face-changing (virtual camera drivers such as OBS Virtual Camera, DeepFaceLive); spectral anomalies in audio stream indicating voice synthesis; interview answers that read as AI-generated; coding challenge submissions from corporate devices |
| CFPF-P2-003: Identity verification evasion | Operators circumvent background checks using facilitator-provided identity documents, KYC bypass services ($30-$200 per identity), and biometric spoofing. Drug testing and in-person verification requirements are evaded through U.S.-based facilitators who appear in person. | Background check results that pass basic SSN validation but fail deeper cross-referencing; identity verification documents with metadata suggesting template-based creation; in-person verification conducted by a different individual than the remote worker |

**Data Sources**: ATS (Applicant Tracking System) logs, background check vendor data, video interview platform analytics, HR onboarding systems, device fingerprinting, IP geolocation.

---

### Phase 3: Positioning

| Technique | Description | Indicators |
|-----------|-------------|------------|
| CFPF-P3-001: Remote access establishment | Upon hiring, operators connect to employer systems through the proxy laptop infrastructure. Remote desktop connections route through Astrill VPN to U.S.-based proxy machines, which then connect to employer VPN/SSO. This creates a layered access chain that masks the operator's true location. | VPN-over-VPN connection patterns; login sessions from U.S. IPs but with timezone-inconsistent activity patterns; remote management tool processes running alongside employer tools; device fingerprint anomalies (OS/hardware mismatches) |
| CFPF-P3-002: Credential and access harvesting | Within hours or days of onboarding, operators begin harvesting credentials, session cookies, API keys, and access tokens from employer systems. Browser credential stores, password managers, and SSO session tokens are primary targets. | Unusual credential store access patterns during onboarding period; session cookie export activity; API key generation requests disproportionate to role requirements; access to systems beyond assigned scope |
| CFPF-P3-003: Multi-operator handoff | Multiple DPRK operators may share a single employment identity, working in shifts to maintain continuous presence. Handoffs are observable through behavioral discontinuities — different communication styles, varying technical proficiency, timezone-inconsistent activity. | Inconsistent writing style in communications across different time periods; login patterns suggesting 24-hour coverage; productivity/quality variations that correlate with shift changes; meeting attendance patterns inconsistent with stated timezone |

**Data Sources**: VPN/SSO authentication logs, endpoint detection and response (EDR), browser extension telemetry, credential vault access logs, communication platform analytics, UEBA (User and Entity Behavior Analytics).

---

### Phase 4: Execution

| Technique | Description | Indicators |
|-----------|-------------|------------|
| CFPF-P4-001: Source code exfiltration | Operators clone entire code repositories to personal GitHub accounts, cloud storage services (Google Drive, Dropbox), or external servers. Proprietary source code, infrastructure configurations, and trade secrets are targeted. This activity often begins within the first 24 hours of access. | Git clone operations for repositories outside assigned scope; large data transfers to external cloud storage; unauthorized personal GitHub repository creation containing company code; bulk download of internal documentation |
| CFPF-P4-002: Credential exfiltration for follow-on access | Harvested credentials and session tokens are exfiltrated for use by other DPRK cyber units (e.g., Lazarus Group) in follow-on intrusion operations. This bridges the employment fraud operation with state-sponsored cyber espionage. | Credential access from non-corporate network segments; session tokens used from geographically impossible locations; authentication events from unfamiliar devices using valid credentials; lateral movement patterns inconsistent with role |
| CFPF-P4-003: Sustained low-profile operation | Some operators maintain employment for months or years, performing minimal legitimate work while extracting salary and maintaining access. Work output is often subpar relative to interview performance, with frequent excuses for missed meetings and delayed deliverables. | Persistent gap between interview assessment scores and code review quality; frequent meeting no-shows or camera-off attendance; low code commit frequency relative to peers; manager escalation patterns for performance issues |

**Data Sources**: Git/version control audit logs, DLP (Data Loss Prevention) systems, cloud access security broker (CASB) logs, EDR telemetry, HR performance management systems, code review analytics, network traffic analysis.

---

### Phase 5: Monetization

| Technique | Description | Indicators |
|-----------|-------------|------------|
| CFPF-P5-001: Salary extraction and conversion | Salary payments are routed to facilitator-controlled bank accounts, then converted to cryptocurrency (primarily USDT/USDC) through PayPal, peer-to-peer exchanges, and over-the-counter brokers. Daily conversion limits are used to avoid triggering AML alerts. Funds ultimately flow to DPRK-controlled accounts. | Salary direct deposit to recently opened accounts; rapid conversion of salary deposits to cryptocurrency; multiple employee accounts converting through the same payment processor; ACH deposits immediately followed by crypto exchange transactions |
| CFPF-P5-002: Post-termination data extortion | After termination or discovery, operators threaten to publish exfiltrated source code, trade secrets, or internal communications unless ransom is paid. This tactic has escalated since mid-2024, with some operators demanding six- and seven-figure payments. | Ransom demands referencing specific internal code or documents; communication from former employee's personal channels containing proprietary information; publication of company code on public repositories as pressure tactic |
| CFPF-P5-003: Credential monetization for cyber operations | Harvested credentials and access tokens are transferred to DPRK cyber units for use in supply chain attacks, cryptocurrency exchange compromises, and espionage operations. This represents the intelligence value beyond direct financial extraction. | Follow-on intrusions using credentials associated with former DPRK IT worker accounts; supply chain compromises linked to previously employed DPRK operatives; cryptocurrency exchange breaches traced to insider credentials |

**Data Sources**: Payroll/ACH transaction monitoring, cryptocurrency exchange transaction records, threat intelligence feeds (DPRK-linked wallet clusters), incident response data, law enforcement liaison, OFAC sanctions screening.

## Look Left / Look Right Analysis

**Discovery Phase**: Typically discovered at **Phase 3 (Positioning)** or **Phase 4 (Execution)** — when security teams detect anomalous VPN patterns, when managers escalate persistent performance issues, or when DLP systems flag bulk code repository downloads. Increasingly discovered during onboarding when enhanced identity verification catches inconsistencies. Some cases are discovered at **Phase 5** through post-termination extortion attempts.

**Look Left** (what was missed before discovery):

- **P4 -> P3**: Were there VPN-over-VPN patterns or timezone-inconsistent login activity that should have triggered UEBA alerts? Were credential vault access patterns during onboarding anomalous?
- **P3 -> P2**: Did the interview process include video verification? Were there discrepancies between interview performance and initial work output? Did background checks cross-reference education credentials with university registrars?
- **P2 -> P1**: Were there red flags in the application — U.S. address paired with non-North American education? Was the LinkedIn profile recently created with few connections? Did the resume show employment gaps inconsistent with claimed experience?
- **Cross-team gap**: HR processes the hire. IT provisions access. Security monitors for threats. Engineering manages code repositories. Finance processes payroll. The DPRK IT worker signal spans all five domains — a holistic view connecting hiring anomalies, access patterns, code access, and financial flows is required but rarely exists in a single team's visibility.

**Look Right** (predicted next steps if uninterrupted):

- Successfully placed operators will maintain employment for 6-18 months, extracting $100K-$300K in salary while harvesting credentials
- Exfiltrated credentials will be transferred to DPRK cyber units (Lazarus Group, Kimsuky) for follow-on supply chain or cryptocurrency exchange attacks
- The same facilitator network will place additional operators at the compromised company and at peer companies
- If terminated without detection, operators will escalate to data extortion within days
- Revenue flows to DPRK weapons development programs in violation of UN Security Council sanctions, creating sanctions compliance liability for employing entities

## Detection Approaches

### Queries / Rules

**SQL — DPRK IT Worker Resume Red Flag Detection (Phase 1-2)**

```sql
SELECT
    a.applicant_id,
    a.full_name,
    a.address_country,
    a.education_country,
    a.education_institution,
    a.linkedin_created_date,
    a.github_created_date,
    bg.ssn_first_issued_date,
    bg.credit_file_depth
FROM applicants a
LEFT JOIN background_checks bg ON a.applicant_id = bg.applicant_id
WHERE a.address_country = 'US'
  AND a.education_country NOT IN ('US', 'CA', 'GB', 'AU', 'NZ', 'IE')
  AND (
    bg.credit_file_depth < 3
    OR bg.ssn_first_issued_date > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '5 years'
    OR a.linkedin_created_date > CURRENT_DATE - INTERVAL '12 months'
  )
ORDER BY a.application_date DESC;
```

**Splunk — VPN/Proxy Anomaly Detection for Remote Workers (Phase 3)**

```spl
index=vpn_auth sourcetype=corporate_vpn
| eval hour_local = strftime(_time, "%H")
| stats count AS login_count,
        values(src_ip) AS source_ips,
        dc(src_ip) AS unique_ips,
        earliest(_time) AS first_login,
        latest(_time) AS last_login
    BY user, date_wday
| where unique_ips > 3 OR (hour_local < 5 AND hour_local > 1)
| lookup ip_reputation src_ip OUTPUT ip_type, vpn_provider
| where ip_type IN ("residential_proxy", "vpn", "datacenter")
    OR vpn_provider = "Astrill"
| table user, source_ips, unique_ips, ip_type, vpn_provider, login_count
| sort - unique_ips
```

**Sigma — Bulk Code Repository Clone Detection (Phase 4)**

```yaml
title: Bulk Code Repository Clone Within First Week
status: experimental
description: Detects a new employee cloning multiple code repositories within their first 7 days, a pattern associated with DPRK IT worker data exfiltration.
logsource:
    product: git_platform
    service: audit_log
detection:
    selection:
        action: "repo.clone"
        actor_tenure_days|lte: 7
    aggregation:
        count|gte: 5
        groupby: actor
        timeframe: 24h
    condition: selection and aggregation
level: high
tags:
    - fraud.dprk_it_worker
    - cfpf.phase4.execution
    - attack.t1005
```

### Behavioral Analytics

- **Interview-to-performance gap analysis**: Compare technical interview assessment scores with post-hire code review metrics, commit quality, and peer feedback scores. Persistent gaps where interview performance significantly exceeds job performance are a key DPRK IT worker indicator.
- **Multi-operator behavioral detection**: Analyze communication patterns (writing style, response timing, vocabulary) across time windows to identify behavioral discontinuities suggesting multiple operators sharing one identity. Machine learning models can detect style shifts that correlate with timezone-based "shift changes."
- **VPN layering detection**: Monitor for VPN-over-VPN connection patterns where the employee connects through a consumer VPN (Astrill) to a U.S. residential IP, which then connects to corporate VPN. Network flow analysis can identify the characteristic latency and hop patterns.
- **Credential access velocity profiling**: Establish baselines for how quickly new employees access credential stores, API key management systems, and internal documentation. Access patterns that deviate significantly from peer baselines during the first week of employment warrant investigation.

### Cross-Team Correlation

- **HR -> Security**: Hiring pipeline anomalies (video interview refusal, education/address mismatches, thin background check profiles) should trigger enhanced monitoring during the onboarding period.
- **Security -> Engineering**: VPN anomalies and credential access alerts should be correlated with code repository access patterns to identify exfiltration campaigns.
- **Engineering -> HR**: Code review quality concerns and persistent performance gaps flagged by engineering managers should be cross-referenced with hiring pipeline data for DPRK indicator patterns.
- **Finance/Compliance -> Security**: Payroll account changes, rapid cryptocurrency conversion patterns, and OFAC screening alerts should trigger security investigation of the associated employee.
- **Legal -> All Teams**: DPRK IT worker discovery triggers sanctions compliance obligations — Legal must coordinate evidence preservation, law enforcement notification, and regulatory disclosure across all teams.

## Analyst Notes

**This is not employment fraud — it is a state-sponsored insider threat program**: The critical distinction between DPRK IT worker operations and conventional employment fraud (TP-0015) is that DPRK operations are directed by a nation-state with intelligence objectives. Salary extraction is the floor — the ceiling is supply chain compromise, cryptocurrency exchange infiltration, and weapons program funding. Organizations that treat this as an HR problem rather than a national security threat will fail to detect or respond effectively.

**The facilitator network is the key infrastructure**: Individual DPRK operators are replaceable; the facilitator network that provides stolen identities, proxy laptop hosting, and financial laundering is the persistent infrastructure. Disrupting facilitator networks has a multiplicative effect — the DOJ's enforcement actions targeting facilitators (Didenko, Phagnasay, Salazar) are more impactful than catching individual operators. Organizations should share facilitator indicators (addresses, bank accounts, identity patterns) with law enforcement and peer companies.

**The escalation to extortion changes the risk calculus**: Pre-2024, DPRK IT worker operations were primarily a sanctions compliance and payroll fraud issue. The evolution to post-termination data extortion means that every successfully placed operator represents a potential data breach and ransom event. Organizations should treat the discovery of a DPRK IT worker as an active incident requiring immediate credential rotation, access revocation, and forensic investigation — not just an HR termination.

**Remote work normalization is the enabling condition**: The post-pandemic shift to remote-first hiring with fully digital onboarding processes has created the conditions for this threat to scale. Many companies have eliminated in-person identity verification, reduced video interview requirements, and normalized asynchronous communication — all of which facilitate DPRK operator concealment. The mitigation is not to eliminate remote work but to implement proportionate identity verification (biometric liveness, credential verification, device attestation) in remote hiring pipelines.

**Sanctions compliance liability is real and immediate**: Under OFAC regulations, organizations that unknowingly employ DPRK nationals and route salary payments to the regime face potential sanctions liability. The "strict liability" nature of sanctions means that lack of knowledge is not a defense. Organizations should integrate OFAC screening into their hiring and payroll processes and establish clear incident response procedures for DPRK IT worker discovery that include legal counsel and regulatory notification.

**Western collaborators represent a qualitatively different detection challenge**: The Flare/IBM X-Force report reveals that some Western participants are knowing collaborators (identity lenders), not unwitting victims of identity theft. Collaborator-enabled placements are significantly harder to detect because the identity documents are genuine — the person exists, the documents are real, and standard identity verification passes cleanly. Detection must shift from identity verification (which catches stolen identities) to behavioral analysis (which catches identity lending — e.g., the employed "person" behaves differently from their historical baseline, or salary payments are split with a third party).

**PurpleBravo/PurpleDelta infrastructure convergence creates compound risk**: Recorded Future's confirmation that DPRK developer-lure campaigns (PurpleBravo/Contagious Interview) share infrastructure with IT worker operations (PurpleDelta) means that a DPRK IT worker placement may simultaneously serve as an entry point for malware deployment targeting the employer's development environment. The BeaverTail infostealer and InvisibleFerret RAT are not just credential theft tools — they represent active, persistent backdoors that can survive the IT worker's termination.

**IC3 2025 Data — Formal IC3 Tracking:** The FBI IC3 2025 Internet Crime Report formally tracks the DPRK IT worker scam. Dozens of victim companies have been identified through IC3.gov complaints. Critically, IC3 confirms that DPRK IT workers are now leveraging unlawful company network access to exfiltrate proprietary data and facilitate cyber-criminal activities — validating the escalation from salary extraction to active insider threat documented in this threat path. PSA250123 (January 23, 2025) covered data extortion, and PSA250723 (July 23, 2025) addressed broader threats to U.S. businesses.

**Cross-border investigation complexity**: DPRK IT worker operations span multiple jurisdictions (DPRK, China, Russia, Ukraine, U.S., EU). Law enforcement coordination requires FBI, CISA, international partners, and private sector threat intelligence sharing. Organizations should establish pre-incident relationships with FBI field offices and CISA regional coordinators to enable rapid response when DPRK IT workers are identified.

**CrowdStrike now tracks 3+ distinct DPRK adversary groups with differentiated operational patterns**: FAMOUS CHOLLIMA (IT worker fraud and GenAI-driven persona fabrication), STARDUST CHOLLIMA (increased operational tempo in 2025), and PRESSURE CHOLLIMA (high-value cryptocurrency exchange theft, including the $1.46B Bybit heist). The differentiation of these groups under separate tracking names suggests organizational separation within DPRK cyber operations — distinct units with distinct missions, TTPs, and targeting — rather than a monolithic program. This has implications for detection: indicators and behavioral patterns effective against FAMOUS CHOLLIMA IT worker placements may not detect PRESSURE CHOLLIMA supply chain compromises, and vice versa. Defenders must maintain detection coverage across all three operational profiles.
